summary: Specifies requirements for an IPv6 Customer Edge router, focusing on basic provisioning of the router and attached hosts, and covers 6rd and Dual-Stack Lite transition. It obsoletes RFC 6204.

eli5.summary: A checklist of what the home router must do to work with the new internet addressing.

questions: what must an ipv6 home router support
what is an ipv6 ce router
subtitle: A baseline checklist of IPv6 features a home or small-office router should support.

tldr.problem: Home and small-office routers need a common baseline for IPv6, so they work with service provider networks and give attached hosts working IPv6 configuration.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists numbered requirements for the router's general behavior, WAN-side provisioning (SLAAC, DHCPv6, prefix delegation), LAN-side configuration, the 6rd and DS-Lite transition technologies, and security.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6204 and has been updated by later RFCs. Its keywords set an industry baseline rather than strict interoperability rules.

facts.label: Max old-prefix Valid Lifetime
facts.value: Lower of current value and two hours

today: RFC 7084 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 6204. It has been updated by RFC 9096 and RFC 9818.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7084 defines basic IPv6 features for a residential or small-office router, called an IPv6 CE router (Customer Edge router), to establish an industry baseline. It covers how the router provisions its WAN interface automatically, acquires address space for its LAN interfaces, and fetches other configuration from the service provider network.

Out of scope are mixed environments where IPv6-only hosts use a translator to reach IPv4 servers, and automatic provisioning of any topology more complex than one router with several LAN interfaces. The RFC also covers two transition technologies: 6rd (RFC 5969) and DS-Lite (RFC 6333).

The RFC 2119 keywords are not used strictly for interoperability here. They establish industry-common baseline functionality, and the document points to other specifications for implementation detail.
sections.eli5: It is a shopping list of IPv6 features a home router should have, so every router works well with internet providers.

sections.title: The End-User Network Model
sections.content:
The model is a stub network: a service provider router connects to the CE router, and the CE router connects one or more LAN links with IPv6 hosts. The IPv6 architecture should provide equivalent or better capabilities than the typical IPv4 setup, a plug-and-play NAT router that blocks incoming connections by default.

Inside the home, link-local addresses serve hosts on one link, and Unique Local Addresses (ULAs, RFC 4193) serve communication across links. The CE router acts as the demarcation point: a ULA boundary, a multicast zone boundary, and ingress and egress traffic filters. Because some hosts cope badly with an IPv6 address but no IPv6 connectivity, the router should not advertise itself as a default router on the LAN when it has no IPv6 connectivity on the WAN.
sections.eli5: The router is the front door of the house. Rooms inside can talk freely, and the router decides what goes out to the street.

sections.title: General and WAN-Side Requirements
sections.content:
General rules include: the router is an IPv6 node (RFC 6434), implements ICMPv6, and MUST NOT forward IPv6 traffic between LAN and WAN until it has completed address and delegated prefix acquisition (G-3). Without a default router on the WAN it MUST NOT advertise itself as a default router on the LAN (G-4), and if it loses one it MUST immediately send Router Advertisements with Router Lifetime zero (G-5).

On the WAN, the router MUST act as an IPv6 host for SLAAC or DHCPv6 address assignment (W-1), finish Duplicate Address Detection before sending Router Solicitations (W-2), use Router Discovery to install a default route (W-3), act as a DHCPv6 prefix delegation requesting router (W-4), and use a persistent DUID that does not change across resets or reboots (W-5). It SHOULD support a Port Control Protocol client (W-6).

For prefix delegation it MAY give a size hint, and if so it MUST ask for enough for one /64 per interface, rounded up to the nearest nibble (WPD-2). It MUST accept a different size than hinted (WPD-3), and by default MUST NOT run a dynamic routing protocol on the WAN (WPD-7). Packets for delegated space that is not assigned to the LAN must be dropped to prevent forwarding loops (WPD-5).
sections.eli5: Facing the internet, the router asks politely for an address and for a big block of addresses to hand out at home. It must wait until it has them before letting traffic through.

sections.title: LAN-Side Requirements
sections.content:
On the LAN, the router SHOULD be able to generate a ULA prefix (ULA-1), MUST keep it consistent across reboots (ULA-2), and by default MUST act as a site border router, filtering packets with local source or destination addresses (ULA-4). If all its prefixes are ULA, it MUST NOT advertise itself as a default router with a nonzero lifetime (ULA-5).

It MUST give each LAN interface a separate /64 from its delegated prefix (L-2) and make each LAN interface an advertising interface (L-5). In Router Advertisements the A and L flags MUST be 1 by default (L-6). It MUST support a DHCPv6 server for addresses or a stateless DHCPv6 server (L-8), and MUST provide DNS information through DHCPv6 (DNS_SERVERS, DOMAIN_LIST) and through Router Advertisement RDNSS and DNS Search List options (L-10, L-11).

If the delegated prefix changes without overlap, the router MUST immediately advertise the old prefix with Preferred Lifetime zero and Valid Lifetime of zero or the lower of the current Valid Lifetime and two hours (L-13). For packets using an invalidated prefix it MUST send ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable, code 5 (L-14).
sections.eli5: Inside the house, the router gives each room its own address block, tells devices where the DNS is, and cleans up neatly if the provider changes the address block.

sections.title: Transition Technologies and Security
sections.content:
The CE router SHOULD support 6rd, and if so it MUST follow RFC 5969. It MUST support configuration through DHCPv4 Option 212 (6RD-1), MUST allow 6rd and native IPv6 WAN interfaces to be active alone or together during migration (6RD-4), and by default MUST prefer native IPv6 when forwarding rules tie (6RD-7).

It SHOULD also support DS-Lite per RFC 6333. It MUST support configuration through the DS-Lite DHCPv6 option (DLW-1) and MUST NOT perform IPv4 NAT on traffic encapsulated using DS-Lite (DLW-2).

On security, the router SHOULD support the recommendations of RFC 6092 (S-1) and SHOULD support BCP 38 ingress filtering (S-2). The RFC notes that S-2 was downgraded from a MUST in RFC 6204 because of implementation difficulty and redundancy with upstream filtering.
sections.eli5: If the provider is still on the older internet, the router can wrap new-style traffic inside old-style traffic, as long as it prefers the new way when both work.
